questions.question: Explain how sociological research can influence social policy, giving examples.

points.text: Sociology influences policy through: evidence (identifying problems), evaluation (assessing effectiveness), advocacy (campaigning for change). Examples: Beveridge (welfare state), Macpherson (police reform), inequality research (minimum wage).

questions.question: Compare positivist and interpretivist views on sociology and social policy.

points.text: Positivists: provide objective evidence for rational policy. Interpretivists: give voice to lived experience. Both contribute: quantitative identifies problems; qualitative shapes solutions.

questions.question: Evaluate whether sociology should aim to influence social policy or remain value-free.

points.text: Value-free: objectivity gives credibility; value-laden: all research is influenced by values anyway; sociology should pursue social justice. Conclusion: transparency about values is essential; research AND advocacy are not mutually exclusive.

questions.question: Full-Mark Response Evaluate the view that sociology should aim to change society rather than just study it. <div class="

points.text: A grade 9 response will: present case for studying (objectivity, credibility); present case for changing (Marx; research improves lives; value-free is impossible); evaluate: studying and changing are not mutually exclusive - rigorous research IS social change; conclude: sociology's primary role is rigorous research, but sociologists should engage with policy and debate. The distinction is a false dichotomy.
